title: A knock on my chamber door in occupied Dresden

blocks.text: Maria Josepha was born on a cold December day in 1699 in Vienna, the first child of Archduke Joseph, the future Emperor, and his wife Wilhelmine Amalie. For a Habsburg, her arrival mattered enormously, because dynasties did not simply have children. They produced heirs, alliances, and future claims. Her sister Maria Amalia followed, and then came the desperately wanted brother, little Leopold Joseph.

But the boy died as a small child, and suddenly the entire future of the monarchy rested on the slender shoulders of two little girls. From the very beginning, Maria Josepha was raised for her rank. She studied Latin and French, was educated in a strictly Catholic environment, and her grandmother Eleonore Magdalene, a deeply pious woman, nurtured the girl’s faith with particular care. That faith would one day define her entire life.

But while her grandmother shaped her soul, the courts of Europe were already calculating her worth. And one man, in particular, had recognized it early. Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, had enormous plans for his son, Frederick Augustus. As early as 1701, when Maria Josepha was barely two years old, he began negotiating a marriage between the little archduchess and his own son. The stakes were immense. Emperor Joseph I had only daughters, and his younger brother Charles was still unmarried. If no more male heirs appeared, Maria Josepha could one day inherit everything. And whoever married her would become one of the most powerful men in Europe. A toddler had become the foundation stone of a European power project. But then everything changed. Maria Josepha’s father died suddenly of smallpox in 1711, just six years after becoming emperor. His brother Charles took the throne as Charles VI.

And now the question of succession became urgent. According to an older family agreement, the daughters of Joseph I would have taken precedence over any future daughters of Charles. That gave Maria Josepha an excellent starting position. Charles VI, naturally, had other ideas. In 1713, he issued the Pragmatic Sanction, a decree that gave his own daughters precedence over the daughters of his late older brother. At the time, Charles had no children at all. His first daughter, the legendary Maria Theresa, would not arrive until 1717. But with her birth, Maria Josepha was suddenly pushed out of the line of succession entirely. Before she was permitted to marry, she had to formally acknowledge the Pragmatic Sanction and renounce all her claims to the Austrian hereditary lands. And that is precisely what she did. On the twentieth of August 1719, after an engagement that had lasted eighteen years, Maria Josepha married the Saxon Crown Prince Frederick Augustus. The political arrangement had been carefully prepared, and even religion had been factored in.

Frederick Augustus had been raised a Protestant but had converted to Catholicism back in 1712, although the news had only been publicly announced later. A Catholic groom was essential, of course, both for Poland, where only a Catholic could reign, and for the marriage to a strictly Catholic Habsburg princess to even be acceptable. When the newlywed couple arrived in Dresden from Vienna, the celebration that followed put everything else in the empire to shame. The wedding festivities stretched across nearly the entire month of September. Banquets, operas, tournaments, hunts, masquerades, and elaborately choreographed stagings transformed the city into a giant stage. One contemporary observer remarked that the Dresden court had become the most magnificent and gallant in the world, everyone acting, everyone playing, everyone being played in turn. Maria Josepha seems to have been genuinely impressed by her new home. And her father-in-law did everything he could to make sure Dresden showed its most splendid face. In honor of the new daughter-in-law, even the famous Zwinger complex was fundamentally transformed. Construction had been underway for about ten years without any fixed overall plan. But when the wedding approached, a problem arose. There were not enough suitable venues for such massive festivities.

So the plans were changed without hesitation. The existing orangery complex was mirrored toward the city side and expanded into a grand festival square. Parts of the Zwinger, which today appears so harmonious, were indeed built quickly, some of them initially in wood, and only replaced with permanent stone constructions years later. When you walk through the Zwinger today, you are walking through a piece of the stage on which a young Habsburg princess was welcomed into her new home. The famous state apartments of the Dresden Royal Palace were likewise furnished especially for this wedding. Destroyed during the Second World War, they have since been elaborately reconstructed, returning visitors to the exact setting created to stage the marriage of a Habsburg princess to the Saxon heir to the throne. But then something happened that was in no way a matter of course in dynastic marriages. The arranged union actually seemed to work. According to surviving reports, Maria Josepha and Frederick Augustus lived in a harmonious marriage, and unlike his father, famous for numerous affairs, Frederick Augustus appears to have had no mistresses at all. One great passion united the couple: hunting. They stayed regularly at the beautiful Moritzburg hunting lodge, where Maria Josepha had her own quarters in three rooms, with her wardrobe in the adjoining tower. Even pregnancies did not keep her from the saddle.

When her son Frederick Christian was born with a physical disability, Maria Josepha blamed herself, connecting it to a fall she had taken from a horse during the pregnancy. Whether there was any real connection cannot be established, of course, but in that era, women were constantly warned to take the greatest care while expecting, and that meant no riding. She gave birth to another child right in Moritzburg, and at first, things looked grim for the little prince as well. According to tradition, he only survived his first hours because a doctor poured Hungarian wine down his throat. That little prince was named Albert Casimir, and he would play a role in Austrian history again. Remember that name. The couple was blessed with a staggering fifteen children. Maria Josepha took intensive care of their upbringing and set strict rules. The family spent a great deal of time together, and the mother personally nursed her sick children, which was by no means common in an age when children had their own staff. And like her cousin Maria Theresa, Maria Josepha proved to be a clever family politician. As early as the 1720s, she proposed a marriage between one of her sons and the young Maria Theresa. Her son Joseph Augustus was to marry the future Habsburg heiress, reuniting the two rival branches of the family in the next generation.

But the plan collapsed when Joseph Augustus died in 1728 at just six years old. And in any case, Charles VI already had another young man in mind for his daughter, a certain Francis Stephen of Lorraine. Still, Maria Josepha’s children would leave their mark on other European dynasties. One daughter became Queen of Spain, another married the Elector of Bavaria. Another daughter, also named Maria Josefa, married the French Dauphin, and through her became the grandmother of three French kings: Louis XVI, Louis XVIII, and Charles X. This relatively unknown woman had stood at the very center of a dynastic network that stretched from Vienna through Dresden and Warsaw all the way to Madrid and Versailles. The year 1733 brought Maria Josepha an entirely new role. When Augustus the Strong died, her husband succeeded him as Elector of Saxony. But the Polish crown was a different matter entirely. Poland was an elective monarchy, and the Wettin position there was by no means secure. After the death of Augustus the Strong, a genuine struggle for the Polish throne broke out. Frederick Augustus ultimately prevailed against his rival Stanislaw Leszczynski, with support from Austria and Russia.

Leszczynski happened to be related to the French king, and as compensation, he was granted the Duchy of Lorraine. That territory, of course, belonged to Francis Stephen, the husband of Maria Theresa, who then had to give it up and received the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in exchange. Leszczynski got Lorraine, Francis Stephen got an elevated title, and Saxony got a kingdom. On the seventeenth of January 1734, Frederick Augustus and Maria Josepha were crowned in Krakow. The Saxon Elector became King Augustus III of Poland, and the Austrian archduchess became a queen. This changed the family’s everyday life completely. The couple now had to divide their time between Saxony and Poland, and the journeys between Dresden and Krakow were anything but comfortable in the eighteenth century. Maria Josepha disliked being separated from her children, so she repeatedly took some of them along on the long journey east. She also made a personal effort to master her new role, learning Polish on top of the many languages she already spoke. And she did not limit herself to representational duties. She followed political developments closely and even took part in parliamentary deliberations in Poland. Her private rooms in the Dresden Royal Palace, set up from 1734, included an audience chamber, a Chinese room, a library, and a concert room.

She held audiences there, read extensively, and delighted in music, which played an enormous role at the Dresden court. In 1733, she received a remarkable birthday gift. Johann Sebastian Bach composed the cantata “Tönet, ihr Pauken! Erschallet, Trompeten! ” in her honor. If that music sounds familiar, there is a reason. Bach later reused parts of it for one of his most famous works, the Christmas Oratorio. A piece of music played around the world every Christmas originally rang out in honor of Maria Josepha. Religion was a difficult subject. Maria Josepha was deeply Catholic, while Saxony was overwhelmingly Protestant. She refused to practice her faith only in private. On her initiative, the Emperor’s Chapel dedicated to Saint Francis Xavier was built in Dresden, and then followed the much grander Catholic Court Church.

Construction began quietly and privately in 1739, and although the church was not yet fully finished, it was consecrated in 1751. The very existence of such a monumental Catholic church in Protestant Dresden carried enormous political and confessional weight. Maria Josepha contributed to parts of its interior, and to this day, one of the most important burial sites of the Wettin dynasty lies in the crypt beneath it. But her religious activity did not stop at church walls. She founded an institution called the Josephinen, using her own funds, to shelter and educate poor and orphaned girls. The remarkable part was this: although the Catholic establishment was founded by a devout Catholic queen, it was explicitly not intended only for Catholic girls. Needy Protestant girls were to be admitted as well. She also supported the founding of a hospital. One of her statements has come down to us and sums up her attitude rather well. When it was pointed out to her that among the many people requesting help there were surely some frauds, she is said to have replied: “It is better to be deceived ten times than, under the pretext of caution, to deny help to even a single truly needy person. ”

Then came the year 1740. Her uncle, Emperor Charles VI, died. And suddenly the very regulation that had determined the course of Maria Josepha’s life decades earlier was put to the test. Maria Theresa claimed the Habsburg inheritance, supported by the Pragmatic Sanction and by the signatures of all the princes of Europe. But after the emperor’s death, those same princes began to question their own agreements. And the first among them was her husband. From a Saxon perspective, the argument went like this: Maria Josepha was the daughter of Joseph I, and Joseph was the older brother of Charles VI. Maria Josepha was also older than Maria Theresa. Although she had formally renounced her claims and acknowledged the Pragmatic Sanction, Saxony now revived its demands. And so, family members found themselves suddenly pitted against each other.

Maria Theresa in Vienna, Maria Josepha in Saxony, and Maria Josepha’s own younger sister Maria Amalia in Bavaria with her husband, Charles Albert. The War of the Austrian Succession followed. In the end, Maria Theresa held her ground in the Habsburg lands. And had she not, the question remains whether Austria might today belong to Saxony. The last years of Maria Josepha’s life were overshadowed by a new and far more destructive war. The Seven Years’ War began, and Frederick II of Prussia, who had once been an ally against Maria Theresa, invaded Saxony. The relationship between Saxony and Prussia had been complicated for years. In 1740, Saxony, Prussia, and Bavaria had joined forces against Maria Theresa, planning to divide parts of the Habsburg lands among themselves. But the alliance broke apart when Frederick II secured Silesia for Prussia and Saxon hopes for territorial gains evaporated. Worse, the now-Prussian Silesia lay directly between Saxony and Poland, separating the king’s two realms. So Saxony switched sides, allied with Austria against Prussia. The former ally had become a bitter enemy.

And that decision was to have devastating consequences. Now it was 1756. Prussian troops marched into Saxony. The Saxon army was no match for the Prussian military machine. Frederick Augustus fled to Poland with his son, where he could at least partly continue to rule. But Maria Josepha stayed in Dresden. And so began the most dramatic phase of her life. Frederick II had the queen watched. Prussian soldiers were stationed in the palace, officially for her protection. In reality, they kept her under constant control. She could no longer leave the palace freely. Her correspondence was monitored, and trusted people around her were gradually replaced.

She still lived in her family’s residence, but she was certainly not free. She was a prisoner of the Prussian occupation inside her own palace. Then came a tense confrontation. Inside the Dresden palace, there was a secret archive. Prussian soldiers demanded access to the war correspondence stored within. But part of the archive lay in Maria Josepha’s personal rooms, and the queen refused to surrender the keys. Only when General Friedrich von Wylich declared that he would, if necessary, resort to force did she finally give in. She had no choice. It is a strange irony of fate. A woman who had come to Saxony as an Austrian archduchess, who had never been universally liked because of her demonstrative Catholicism, now stood up to the foreign occupiers. And because of that, the perception of her in Saxony changed enormously. People who had once criticized her now respected the woman who had stayed when her country was occupied.

But Maria Josepha would never see her husband again. Just about a year after the Prussian invasion, on the seventeenth of November 1757, still in occupied Dresden, she died at the age of fifty-seven. According to tradition, the cause of death was a stroke, an instantaneous cardiac death. She was laid to rest in the very church whose construction she had personally supported, the Catholic Court Church. Her tomb remains there today and may still be visited. Her husband died six years later and was buried in the same crypt. But the story does not quite end there. Do you remember the little boy who was born in Moritzburg in 1738, the one who survived his first hours only thanks to Hungarian wine? Albert Casimir of Saxony, son of Maria Josepha. Years later, he fell in love with a Habsburg archduchess, Maria Christina, the favorite daughter of Maria Theresa. And with that, a circle closes. Maria Josepha had once tried to marry one of her sons to Maria Theresa, and that plan had failed.

Decades later, another son of Maria Josepha married a daughter of Maria Theresa. We know Albert and Maria Christina today through an important legacy. They became the founders of one of Vienna’s greatest art collections, the Albertina, named for the two of them. And so the story of Maria Josepha leads back to Vienna in the end, preparing the beginning of an entirely new narrative.
